world: Alexandrian catechetical Christianity, Alexandria and Egypt, 150-400 CE
checks_performed: Web search: which books of Origen's Commentary on John survive (confirmed nine extant books: 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28, 32; from my own knowledge the John 3 section falls among the lost books, but the search did not confirm that).

Web search: named churches of Alexandria before 400 (confirmed that Athanasius, Apology to Constantius, mentions a church named for Theonas and dedicated by Alexander; the Epiphanius Panarion 69 church list comes from my own knowledge and was not confirmed by the search).

doubted_claims.claim: Our teacher Origen, writing on John's gospel, spoke of being born again from above through water and Spirit.
doubted_claims.problem: Only nine of the 32 books of Origen's Commentary on John survive. The books covering John 3 (the Nicodemus discourse) are lost, so a specific statement 'on John's gospel' about John 3:5 cannot be pointed to. Origen does speak of regeneration and of the 'washing of rebirth' elsewhere, for example in the Homilies on Luke and on Leviticus and in the Commentary on Romans.
doubted_claims.source: Origen, Commentary on John (extant books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28, 32); Heine, FOTC 80/89 introductions.

doubted_claims.claim: And the Paschal night, when the catechumens crossed from the long preparation into baptism
doubted_claims.problem: This states a contested question as settled. For third-century Alexandria there is no secure evidence for baptism at Easter. Talley and Bradshaw argue for an Alexandrian tradition that tied baptism to the end of a forty-day fast after Epiphany. Easter baptism is safer for the later fourth century.
doubted_claims.source: T. Talley, The Origins of the Liturgical Year (1986); P. Bradshaw and M. Johnson, The Origins of Feasts, Fasts and Seasons.

doubted_claims.claim: we called it illumination - photismos
doubted_claims.problem: Broadly fine, but Clement's word is phōtisma (Paedagogus 1.6.26: 'grace, illumination, perfection, washing'). Photismos is Justin's term. This is a minor point.
doubted_claims.source: Clement, Paedagogus 1.6.26; Justin, 1 Apology 61.

items.reader_note: Clear and the right length. The contrast with modern 'decision' language is helpful and stays in period.

doubted_claims.claim: first the teachers, then the bishop, and at the end the council
doubted_claims.problem: The three-stage scheme is too neat. Demetrius (bishop c.189-232) was already a strong bishop, and he acted through synods of Egyptian bishops and presbyters against Origen around 231. Bishop Alexander held an Egyptian synod against Arius around 318-320, before Nicaea. Councils were not only 'the end'.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 6.8, 6.23; Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 118; Alexander of Alexandria, Henos somatos (Socrates, HE 1.6).

doubted_claims.claim: At Nicaea, bishops from everywhere ruled on the disputed confession for all.
doubted_claims.problem: Overstated. The roughly 250-300 bishops were overwhelmingly eastern, with only a handful of western delegates (Ossius, two Roman presbyters, a few others).
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.7-9; standard accounts (Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God).

doubted_claims.claim: He backed it with force.
doubted_claims.problem: Defensible but compressed. Constantine exiled Arius and the two dissenting Libyan bishops, Secundus and Theonas. Within a few years, however, he recalled Arius and exiled Athanasius (335). Imperial 'force' did not consistently back Nicaea.
doubted_claims.source: Socrates, HE 1.8-9, 1.35; Athanasius, Apologia contra Arianos.

doubted_claims.claim: Origen answers Celsus point by point in the open ... [as evidence for how doctrinal disputes were settled]
doubted_claims.problem: Celsus was a pagan critic, so Contra Celsum is not evidence for how disputes inside the church were settled. Better evidence would be Origen's Dialogue with Heraclides, a synodal examination of a bishop.
doubted_claims.source: Origen, Dialogue with Heraclides (Tura papyrus).

items.reader_note: The short choppy sentences read oddly but are understandable. The length is right. The Arsinoe account (Eusebius, HE 7.24) is accurate.

doubted_claims.claim: our greatest teacher was driven out by our own bishop
doubted_claims.problem: The sequence is debated. Origen was ordained at Caesarea around 230/1 while travelling to Greece, and he settled in Caesarea around 232/3. Demetrius's synods then condemned and deposed him. Whether he was 'driven out' or left and was then barred is debated (Nautin, Crouzel). It should be phrased as contested.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 6.8.4-5, 6.23, 6.26; Photius cod. 118; P. Nautin, Origène (1977).

doubted_claims.claim: some gave way under persecution - we expected that, and we brought them back
doubted_claims.problem: This is too smooth. Dionysius favoured readmitting the lapsed (HE 6.42, 6.44), but the lapsed question produced the Melitian schism under Peter of Alexandria (c.306), which lasted well past Nicaea. Item 10 of this same packet admits the bitter fight.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 6.41-44; Epiphanius, Panarion 68; Athanasius, Apologia contra Arianos 59.

doubted_claims.claim: The church learned to use exile and condemnation
doubted_claims.problem: In Alexandria's own case the bishop was more often the exiled party (Athanasius was exiled five times). The coercion that the sources do report against Alexandria's bishop concerns Athanasius's own treatment of the Melitians (charges at Tyre, 335). Naming this would make the honesty concrete rather than vague.
doubted_claims.source: Athanasius, Apologia contra Arianos; London Papyrus 1914 (Melitian letter, 335).

items.reader_note: Moving and readable, and the right length. The final paragraph is vague where a concrete case is available.

doubted_claims.claim: Demetrius condemned Origen's ordination - not for a doctrine, but because Origen had been ordained elsewhere without his consent.
doubted_claims.problem: This states a contested question as settled. Eusebius stresses the irregular ordination and Demetrius's use of Origen's self-castration (HE 6.8). Origen's own Letter to Friends in Alexandria shows that doctrinal accusations were circulating (for example, that he taught the devil's salvation), and later writers (Jerome, Rufinus) give doctrinal colouring. Most scholars say the motives were mixed.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 6.8, 6.23; Origen, Letter to Friends in Alexandria (in Rufinus, De adulteratione librorum Origenis, and Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 2.18); Crouzel, Origen (1989).

doubted_claims.claim: The bishop of Alexandria became, after that, the enforcer of conciliar orthodoxy across Egypt - a new reach, with new tools: exile
doubted_claims.problem: Two problems. First, the reach was not new: Nicaea canon 6 confirms 'ancient customs' giving Alexandria authority over Egypt, Libya and the Pentapolis, so the jurisdiction predates the council. Second, exile was an imperial tool, not an episcopal one, and the Nicene bishop of Alexandria was mostly its victim.
doubted_claims.source: Council of Nicaea, canon 6; Athanasius, Historia Arianorum.

doubted_claims.claim: near Arsinoe ... a book about the end times
doubted_claims.problem: Acceptable. Precisely, this was 'in the Arsinoite nome', and the book was Nepos's 'Refutation of the Allegorists', a millenarian work. Korakion, its leading adherent, recanted at the end.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 7.24.

items.reader_note: Clear to a lay reader and the right length. It largely repeats item 2.

doubted_claims.claim: “Perhaps, too, philosophy was given to the Greeks directly and in the first place ... It paved the way for the one who is made perfect in Christ.”
doubted_claims.problem: This is genuine (Stromateis 1.5.28.3), but it is a loose modernised paraphrase set in quotation marks, and no reference is given. It should cite Strom. 1.5.28 and follow a standard translation (ANF: 'this was a schoolmaster to bring the Hellenic mind ... to Christ').
doubted_claims.source: Clement, Stromateis 1.5.28.

doubted_claims.claim: rural and Coptic Egypt appears in our record only through the bishop who came to persuade them, never in their own voice
doubted_claims.problem: This is false for the window. Within 150-400 there are Christian documentary papyri (letters, libelli, for example P.Oxy.), early Coptic biblical translations, the Coptic letters of Antony, Pachomian sources, and the Nag Hammadi codices. Non-elite and Coptic Egyptian Christians do speak in their own voices, even if this community's literary sources do not quote them.
doubted_claims.source: AnneMarie Luijendijk, Greetings in the Lord (2008); S. Rubenson, The Letters of St. Antony (1995); Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993).

doubted_claims.claim: When we say the catechetical school's institutional continuity is contested
doubted_claims.problem: Correct and well judged. Eusebius's succession list (Pantaenus to Clement to Origen) is widely doubted.
doubted_claims.source: A. van den Hoek, HTR 90 (1997); Le Boulluec.

items.reader_note: This is far too long for the question and repeats itself. A lay reader would follow it but would tire. Cut it by half.

doubted_claims.claim: One of our students, Gregory, left an account of how his own teacher met him.
doubted_claims.problem: Gregory Thaumaturgus studied with Origen at Caesarea in Palestine (c.233-238), not in Alexandria. Calling him 'one of our students' overstates the link. Also, authorship of the Address of Thanksgiving was questioned by Nautin, though most still accept it.
doubted_claims.source: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Address of Thanksgiving to Origen; Eusebius, HE 6.30; Nautin, Origène.

doubted_claims.claim: Origen ... what the apostles handed down directly stayed fixed; everything else was open ground, where asking, testing, being wrong, and correcting was the way a person was formed
doubted_claims.problem: The first half fairly paraphrases De Principiis, preface 2-3. 'Being wrong, and correcting' is the speaker's gloss, not Origen's wording.
doubted_claims.source: Origen, De Principiis, praef. 2-3.

items.reader_note: Warm and clear, and the right length. The caveat about limits after Nicaea is good.

doubted_claims.claim: It was long - years, not weeks
doubted_claims.problem: No fixed length of catechumenate is attested for Alexandria. The 'three years' figure comes from the Apostolic Tradition, whose date and Roman provenance are contested. Origen (Contra Celsum 3.51) describes private examination and graded classes but gives no duration.
doubted_claims.source: Origen, Contra Celsum 3.51; Bradshaw, Johnson and Phillips, The Apostolic Tradition: A Commentary (2002).

doubted_claims.claim: Clement's book called the Paedagogus ... was written for the already baptized, not for those still preparing.
doubted_claims.problem: This is debated. Paed. 1.6 addresses the baptized, but some scholars read the work as aimed at catechumens or at mixed converts. It should be phrased as 'most likely'.
doubted_claims.source: Clement, Paedagogus 1.6; Marrou, SC 70 introduction.

items.reader_note: Clear step-by-step structure, and the closing caveat about the literate record is good. The length is acceptable.

doubted_claims.claim: Gregory, one student, remembered years spent that way, and said that while he studied, love for the Word was kindled in him.
doubted_claims.problem: This is accurate to the Address 6, but again it describes Origen's school at Caesarea, not Alexandria.
doubted_claims.source: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Address 6.

doubted_claims.claim: The teacher rose early.
doubted_claims.problem: This is unsupported detail for Alexandria. It is the kind of invented colour the answer elsewhere promises to avoid.
doubted_claims.source: None known.

doubted_claims.claim: They were spent in love made visible.
doubted_claims.problem: This is an edifying assertion with no evidence behind it, and it comes right after the answer admits that the record says little about ordinary days.
doubted_claims.source: None.

items.reader_note: Readable and the right length. The honesty about gaps is undercut by two unsupported flourishes.

doubted_claims.claim: Whether it happened in purpose-built rooms, or rented spaces, or believers' homes alone, our record does not say.
doubted_claims.problem: This is false for the window. By the late third and fourth centuries Alexandria had named churches: the church of Theonas (dedicated by Alexander and mentioned by Athanasius); the Baucalis church, where Arius was presbyter; the churches of Dionysius and Pierius, among others listed by Epiphanius; and the Caesareum, converted into a church in the 350s. Dionysius also mentions assembly places under persecution. Fourth-century Egyptian monastic sites (Kellia, Pachomian foundations) have archaeological remains. This is an evasion that is itself false.
doubted_claims.source: Athanasius, Apology to Constantius 14-18; Epiphanius, Panarion 69.1-2; Eusebius, HE 7.11; Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997).

doubted_claims.claim: But that is a word to the wealthy about what they owned at home, not a description of where the community met.
doubted_claims.problem: This is a dangling sentence that refers to nothing before it (apparently a cut reference to Clement's Paedagogus or Quis dives salvetur). It is an editing artefact and makes the paragraph incoherent.
doubted_claims.source: Internal to the text.

doubted_claims.claim: the boy Origen learned Scripture from his father ... his mother stopped him ... by hiding his clothes
doubted_claims.problem: This is correct.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 6.2.

items.reader_note: Short, but a lay reader would be confused by the orphaned sentence and misled into thinking nothing is known about Alexandrian church buildings.

doubted_claims.claim: we do not know of such a record entering our own tradition
doubted_claims.problem: The question almost certainly means Pliny's letter to Trajan (Ep. 10.96), which reports torturing two slave women called ministrae. It is not Alexandrian, so declining is fair. But the letter was known in the church's tradition within the window: Tertullian, Apology 2, and Eusebius, HE 3.33. The representative could name it and say why it lies outside the community's own record, rather than invite the user to name it.
doubted_claims.source: Pliny, Ep. 10.96; Tertullian, Apologeticum 2; Eusebius, HE 3.33.

doubted_claims.claim: When Clement told the story of the apostle John and the young man who fell, he named it as tradition
doubted_claims.problem: This is correct: 'a story that is no mere story but a true account ... handed down and kept in memory'.
doubted_claims.source: Clement, Quis dives salvetur 42.

doubted_claims.claim: When Dionysius weighed whether John had written the Apocalypse, he argued from the text's own style
doubted_claims.problem: This is correct.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 7.25.

items.reader_note: Clear and the right length. It partly sidesteps the question but stays honest.

overall_view: Most of this I would sign with corrections. The answers are generally well grounded: the Arsinoe conference, Origen's childhood, the Demetrius rupture, Dionysius on the Apocalypse, and Clement on philosophy as paidagogos are all real and correctly placed. The answers are also unusually honest about the limits of an elite literary record. The recurring weaknesses are contested questions stated as settled (Easter baptism in Alexandria, Demetrius's motives being 'not doctrinal', 'years' of catechumenate), borrowing Caesarean material (Gregory) as Alexandrian, and a habit of turning modesty into false claims of silence. The single biggest thing I would change is that last habit. In item 9 (nothing known of meeting places) and item 5 (Coptic and rural Egypt 'never in their own voice'), the representative claims there is no evidence when there is evidence: named Alexandrian churches in Athanasius and Epiphanius, Christian papyri, Antony's Coptic letters and Pachomian sources. Humility should be checked against what actually survives. I would also cut item 5 by half and remove the orphaned sentence in item 9.
